reason: C code. 51degrees-cxx ignores a single header longer than the maximum matched User-Agent length (src/dd/results-dd.h, bufferPseudoLength), so the crates find no device for a 2,000 character User-Agent. The .NET package builds older C code, which matches the start of it. Judged again once the .NET packages build the same 51degrees-cxx release.

C code. 51degrees-cxx looks up an address in ::ffff:0:0/96 as the IPv4 address it holds (RFC 4291 section 2.5.5.2, src/ipi/ipi.c), so ::ffff:1.1.1.1 gives 1.1.1.1's network. The older C code the .NET package builds does not. Judged again once the .NET packages build the same 51degrees-cxx release.
A sequence .NET cannot read as a 32-bit integer gives an error from the Sequence element and another from the JSON builder, which then writes nothing. The crates give no error and carry on.
The JSON builder in .NET writes nothing when the sequence in the evidence is not a 32-bit integer.
The sequence after 2147483647 wraps to a negative 32-bit number in .NET, so JavaScript properties are still listed. The crates hold a 64-bit sequence.
The crates hold the sequence as a 64-bit integer and start again at 1 for a sequence that is not a number, where .NET holds a 32-bit integer and leaves a bad value as it was.
The crates' Sequence element writes the session id and sequence into its own data, where .NET writes them back into the evidence.
The crates' Sequence element lists the session id and sequence as properties of its own data. .NET's lists none.
The JSON builder writes the data of the crates' Sequence element, which .NET's Sequence element does not have.
With no address in the evidence the crates' IP Intelligence engine gives an error and no data, where .NET gives data in which no property has a value.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine gives an error when the evidence holds no address it can read. .NET gives none.
The JSON builder writes the IP Intelligence error the crates give when the evidence holds no address it can read.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine writes no data when the evidence holds no address it can read, so the JSON has no ip object.
The crates do not fill the Ip property with the address looked up, as .NET does.
The crates do not fill the IpV6 property with the address looked up, as .NET does.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine lists a fixed set of property names whatever the data file holds. The ASN file holds few of them.
Every Device Detection property with no value gives the same sentence and IP Intelligence gives none of .NET's reasons.
The crates take Device Detection property types from a table compiled into the crate rather than from the data file, so the JavaScript properties are strings.
With no User-Agent the crates give an empty string where .NET gives no value, and the screen sizes have no value where .NET gives 0.
The JSON holds the empty strings the crates give where .NET gives no value (properties.device state).
The crates' JSON builder leaves out a property with no value, where .NET writes null and a nullreason entry.
The crates' JSON builder sorts element keys and property names, where .NET keeps their order.
The crates' JSON builder lists JavaScript properties in name order, where .NET keeps the property order.
The JavaScript holds the JSON, so every JSON difference shows here too, and the template output has its own differences.
The crates have no public sink for usage records yet, so the Rust producer writes none.
